An order to open the rift beneath his war-camp." Her smile turned wistful.
"It took me three weeks to master your penmanship!
Your loops are atrocious, by the way...
A goddess ought to take more care."
"Ellvi," Eluned choked out, her fingers weakly clawing at the black roots.
"The roots.
You have unsealed the—"
CRUNCH!
The massive roots twisted violently and pulled Eluned down into the gaping lightless chasm that had opened in the heartwood floor.
Ellvi leaned over the edge to watch her sister go, and then, with the tip of a polished boot, nudged a fallen star-lotus crown in after her.
"You won’t be needing that," she said.
"I’m redecorating."
The World Tree shuddered with a colossal groan echoing from deep within its core as Lady Eluned was absorbed into the wood.
The instant she vanished, a tidal wave of golden-green mana erupted from the chasm and rushed straight into Ellvi’s chest.
Ellvi arched her back, throwing her head toward the stormy sky as the stolen power flooded her veins.
"Lady Ellvi!" Captain Kaelith shouted, stepping forward with her tower shield raised and her voice shaking with disbelief.
"What is this?!
How is this possible?!
Release the Lady!"
Ellvi slowly lowered her head and looked at the eight shieldmaidens with venomous disdain.
She wiped a drop of golden blood from her cheek with her thumb, regarded it with distaste, and wiped it on the elder’s sleeve beside her.
"Good riddance," she sneered, in a cold purr.
"For a thousand years her timid, saintly presence has been a thorn in my side...
She held all this authority, yet she wept over dead leaves and refused to conquer the outer rings and you, Captain.
I knew you would come back early...
I planned for eight guards the way a gardener plans for weeds...
A rest day was never going to hold you."
She smiled at the squad.
"Now.
Why don’t you all die for me?"
She snapped her fingers.
BOOM!
A colossal dome of pressurized green mana exploded from Ellvi’s palm.
The shockwave hit the guards like a falling mountain, and Ther’Abella didn’t even have time to raise her polearm before the blast wave crushed her chest.
SNAP!
CRACK!
WHOOSH!
The force tore her arms from their sockets, shattered the bones in her forearms, and snapped her legs like brittle twigs.
The violent pressure ripped her off the sanctum platform and launched her body into the open sky above the canopy.
Spinning in the air, she caught one last glimpse of the terrace as her sisters were lifting their heads in the rain, and in their eyes, a sickly green light beginning to kindle...
Wind screamed in her ears and rain whipped across her face as she hurtled through the air toward the sprawling metropolis of the lower rings.
’Heal!’ her mind screamed through the blinding red haze. ’Circulate the mana!’
With a desperate ragged gasp, Ther’Abella forced her sluggish core to turn.
Green healing mana surged through her crushed limbs and dragged broken bone fragments back into place with sickening crunches.
She gritted her teeth until her gums bled, twisting her torso in mid-air to orient her boots toward the ground.
KABOOM!
Ther’Abella slammed into the center of a wide commercial plaza and blew a smoking crater into the granite pavers.

Stone fragments sprayed in all directions, shattering shop windows and tearing through awnings and Ther’Abella lay in the middle of the depression, vomiting blood onto the wet stone with her chest heaving as she struggled to push herself upright.
Ugh...
Help..."
’Lady Eluned,’ she thought with her vision blurring. ’Ellvi took her.’
The rain continued to hammer the plaza.
An amplified thunderous voice rolled across the entire district, echoing from the high towers along the bough.
"Citizens of Yggdrasil!
The traitor Ther’Abella of the Viridian Guard has struck down our Lady!
She conspired in secret with the dark forces that took our beloved Overlord a year ago!
She is armed, dangerous, and carries silver hair and a moonlight spear!
Find her!
Bring her head to the roots!"
Ther’Abella pushed herself onto her knees with horror clamping around her throat.
’That will never work,’ she reasoned frantically, coughing up another clot of red. ’The people know us...
They know Lady Eluned’s gentleness...
They would never—’
"Officer?"
A soft hesitant voice spoke from the edge of the crater.
An elderly elven merchant in a leather apron stood at the rim and she recognized his kind face from her morning patrols.
He reached out a weathered hand and stepped down the slope of the rubble toward her.
"Are you hurt, child?
Let me help you up."
Ther’Abella felt a surge of relief.
"Sir, please, you have to hear me.
Lady Ellvi is lying—"
The old man froze mid-step as his eyes went wide.
FZZZZT!
A sickly bright green glare ignited within his pupils and the welcoming hand did not grasp her fingers.
His fingernails lengthened into rigid wooden talons that stabbed straight for her jugular.
’No!’
Years of drills fired on instinct.
Ther’Abella threw her upper body backward and pressed her palms into the wet rock, and the wooden claws sliced through the air an inch above her nose, tearing the silver collar of her tunic.
Above the plaza, Ellvi’s voice roared from the towers, dripping with toxic command.
"IF YOU WISH TO LIVE, KILL HER!
SHE KILLED YOUR OVERLORD!
TEAR HER APART!"
Around the crater, dozens of elves, guards, merchants, and women carrying market baskets, turned their heads at the same moment.
Every pair of eyes ignited with the same unnatural green light.
"DIE!"
"TRAITOR!"
"AVENGE THE OVERLORD!"
They surged down the crater like a pack of rabid animals, pulling cleavers, iron ladles, and ornamental daggers from their belts.
A blast of wind-mana erupted from an incoming city guard and hurled a cluster of jagged stone spikes straight at her face.
Ther’Abella rolled aside, snatched her polearm from the mud, and watched the spikes obliterate the flagstones where she had been lying.
’They’re insane,’ she thought, scrambling to her feet. ’I have to run.’

She channeled wind-mana into her calves as a concentrated updraft blasted from the soles of her boots and launched her straight up out of the crater, over the grasping hands and onto the tiled roof of a three-story tea house.
Three enchanted arrows whistled through the downpour with their tips glowing with acidic green venom however she spun her polearm in a tight vertical circle.
CLANG!
CLANG!
TING!
The silver blade knocked two arrows into the rain gutters, and the third clipped her shoulder pauldron, hissing as it dissolved a layer of lacquer.
Down in the streets, hundreds of green-eyed elves poured out of alleyways and climbed the trellises and drainpipes with inhuman agility.
Spells of fire, pressurized water, and earth-spikes began bombarding the rooftops, blowing timber and ceramic shingles into flying shrapnel.
She sprinted.
WHOOSH!
Her boots slapped wet clay tiles as she leaped across narrow alleys, using small precise pulses of wind beneath her feet to glide between rooftops.
BOOM!
A bolt of lightning vaporized a brick chimney behind her.

She ducked under a sweeping wave of flame, cut a thrown cleaver out of the air with the flat of her blade, and vaulted a bunch of earth-spikes with a Gale Step that left a ring of shattered tile in her wake.
Behind her the mob grew by the minute, because the towers kept calling and the whole city kept answering.

Ahead stood an elite squad of the royal palace guard, blocking the massive suspension bridge that led toward the city limits was an officer in a shimmering mantle that warped the light around his shoulders, with the crest of Princess Selvanie embroidered along the hem.
’The Spatial Cloak,’ Ther’Abella realized. ’It belongs to Princess Selvanie’s private retinue...’
That cloak was an enchanted relic capable of short-range spatial translocation.
If she could take it, she could bypass the city walls.
"STOP HER!" the officer shouted, drawing his rapier as his eyes flared green.
Ther’Abella didn’t slow down.
She leaped from the edge of the roof, wrapping her wind-mana around her body like a descending cyclone, and slammed into the center of the bridge.
Her polearm swept low with the haft catching two guards behind their knees and dropping them.
The officer’s rapier flickered toward her throat in three thrusts too fast to follow.
WHOOSH!
WHOOSH!
WHOOSH!

Ther’Abella turned the first with her haft, took the second across her cheek, and bent beneath the third, and before he could trigger the blade’s enchantment she closed the distance in one step, drove her shoulder into his sternum, and ripped the silver clasp of the Spatial Cloak clean off his collar.
"Traitor!" the officer choked out.
She threw the shimmering cloak around her shoulders, channeled raw mana into the hem, and pulled the hood forward.
VRRRRR-POP!
Space folded as the bridge, the screaming guards, and the rain-slicked roofs vanished into a silent blur of violet light.
’Take me out of here please...’
THUD!
Ther’Abella tumbled out of the spatial rift with her knees in muddy grass.
She was outside the city and ahead of her, rising against the dark, stormy horizon, were the colossal Outer Boundary Gates of Yggdrasil.

These were the dimensional portals at the very edge of the World Tree’s territory massive arched structures of ancient petrified wood intertwined with crystalline vines that hummed with a deep blue light.
They led outward, connecting the secluded realm of the elves to the wild sectors of the Sovereign Realm beyond and they were dying.

Because Lady Eluned had been torn from the tree’s core, the energy sustaining the gates was failing as the blue light sputtered, fading into a dull ash-gray, and the portals shrank and their edges contracting inward like burning paper.
’I have to cross,’ she thought, staggering to her feet and dragging her polearm through the mud. ’If I stay here, they will butcher me...
I have to reach the Sovereign Realm, get stronger, and come back for Lady Eluned...’
She took three running steps toward the nearest archway.
THWIP-BOOM!
An explosive arrow struck the ground five feet in front of her.
The concussive force hurled Ther’Abella backward, and she planted her blade into the soil to stop her momentum, panting as she wiped the rain from her eyes.
Through the mist, seven armored figures walked forward and cut off the path to the gates.
Ther’Abella’s heart stopped.
Standing in a loose semicircle were the surviving members of the Viridian Guard.
’Why... why are they here...?’
Captain Kaelith stood in the center with her tower shield on her left arm and her two-handed battleaxe in her right with the stance she called the Hollow Oak.
Flanking her were Caelia and Evandra, the twin blade-dancers, their curved scimitars drawn and humming with pressurized wind.
Behind them stood the three elite archers, Althea, Nim, and Cheryl with their composite bows fully drawn, holding explosive arrowheads trained on Ther’Abella’s chest.
To the far right stood Moriel, the spear-master, her long crystalline lance held in a relaxed low guard.
It was the formation they had drilled ten thousand times.
Ther’Abella knew every angle of it, which was exactly why she knew she could not win.

Kaelith’s shield denied the center, the twins covered both flanks with overlapping arcs, Moriel’s lance owned the long middle distance, and the archers sat behind them like three patient stones, covering every gap the others left.
In drills, the youngest member had never once broken it because in those same drills, they had always held back.

chapters.title: Chapter 649: Too Weak To Save Them
paragraphs: In all of their eyes that same sickening green light was burning.
Yet, unlike the civilians in the city, their glare wasn’t solid... It flickered wildly, dimming and flaring like a torch struggling against a gale.

"Captain," Ther’Abella whispered, taking a trembling step forward with her polearm lowering slightly. "Caelia... Moriel... Please... Look at me... It’s Ther’Abella, Ellvi took the core and she sealed Lady Eluned into the heartwood. We have to go back together."
"Ther..."
Captain Kaelith’s mouth cracked open.
Her teeth were locked so tightly that blood seeped between her lips and ran down her chin as her hands trembled on the haft of her axe with her knuckles white as she fought her own limbs.
"Kill us," Kaelith choked out, her voice turning into a strangled croak. "Ther’Abella, please... We can’t hold it back much longer."
Ther’Abella shook her head, tears spilling down her cheeks and mixing with the rain.
"I can’t kill you! I can’t kill any of you! We took our vows together beneath the blooming bough! We swore to support Lady Eluned with our lives! We’re sisters!"
"YOU WILL DIE!"
A harsh screeching voice tore from Moriel’s throat as the green light in her eyes flared blinding.
The spear-master crossed the distance in the blink of an eye.
SWOOSH-SLAM!
The crystalline lance thrust straight for Ther’Abella’s throat, then split into three strikes before she could register the first.
This was Moriel’s Crystal Needle, a technique that had once pinned a rift-wyrm to a cliff face.

Ther’Abella deflected the first thrust by a fraction of an inch, tilted her skull to let the second whisper past her ear, and felt the third punch through her shoulder pauldron and into the meat beneath.
BOOM!
She sucked in a breath through her teeth as the force behind the blow jarred her already damaged shoulder and sent a spike of agony down her spine.
Before she could recover, Captain Kaelith stepped into the pocket with terrifying speed with her shield forward and her axe back.
"DIE, TRAITOR!" Kaelith’s voice boomed, though tears streamed from the corners of her green-lit eyes.

The shield hammered into Ther’Abella’s chest and drove the wind out of her, and in the half-second she spent stunned, the axe came down in a vertical cleave that whistled with enough force to split a boulder.
This was the Rootbreaker... It was something everyone was really familiar with.
Ther’Abella dropped flat against the mud and rolled hard to her right.
KABOOM!
The greataxe cleaved into the bedrock beneath the soil and sent a shower of jagged stone and mud into the air.
Kaelith wrenched it free without a single pause because pausing was something the Captain had never in her life done in battle.
SHING! SHING!
From the left and right, Caelia and Evandra closed in seamlessly.
The twin blade-dancers moved with terrifying synchronization with their scimitars weaving a net of razor-sharp wind that sealed off every direction.
Their Gale Cross had once shredded an assault force of forty as the scimitars crossed above her head like scissors closing.
SHCK!
Ther’Abella twisted her torso, but one scimitar sliced clean through the meat of her left thigh while the other carved a deep red furrow across her ribs and blood sprayed into the mud.
"Ther, run," Evandra sobbed even as her arms snapped into a reverse grip and drove both scimitars down toward Ther’Abella’s neck.
"I CAN’T!" Ther’Abella screamed through her teeth.
Behind the twins, the three archers fired in staggered rhythm, and the first volley alone would have shredded a lesser fighter.
They called it Thornfall... Three arrows loosed on three different arcs that landed within a heartbeat of one another, each one angled so that dodging the first would walk her into the second.
Althea’s arrow was a pinning shot, aimed at the mud beside her hand to lock her cloak to the earth.
Nim’s was a homing arrow that bent in the rain to find her and Cheryl’s arrowhead exploded on contact.
WHOOSH! WHOOSH! WHOOSH!
Between them they never left a gap wider than a breath, and each arrow was angled to herd Ther’Abella back toward the center, where the twins were waiting.
’T-this...’
She cut one out of the air, felt another graze her hip, and understood with cold clarity that she was not fighting seven broken women.
She was fighting the finest squad in the Sovereign Realm, and every one of them was still fighting well...
If she didn’t fight, she would die here and if she died here, no one would ever know the truth.
’This...’
Lady Eluned would remain trapped in that dark suffocating chasm for eternity, remembered as a traitor who had killed someone she had viewed as her own brother.
’Forgive me.’
Ther’Abella planted her left hand in the mud and channeled her wind-mana.
FWOOM!
A concussive shockwave erupted from her palm, blasting the mud outward and jarring the twins’ balance for half a second.
In that tiny opening, she pivoted on her good knee and swung her silver polearm in a horizontal arc.
The blade caught Caelia across the chest, carved through her leather cuirass, and sliced deep into her lungs.
Before Evandra could scream, Ther’Abella used the rotational momentum of the swing to drive the iron-capped butt of the weapon upward into Evandra’s chin.
CRACK!
Evandra’s neck snapped backward and both sisters collapsed into the mud with their blood mingling in the cold puddle.
As the green light faded from Caelia’s dying eyes, she looked up through the rain.
"Thank you," Caelia whispered, her breath rattling out in a final quiet sigh.
Evandra’s hand twitched once against her sister’s sleeve, and then both went still.
THWIP-THWIP-THWIP!
Three explosive arrows tore through the downpour.
One punched through Ther’Abella’s left bicep, detonating on exit and tearing the muscle from the bone and the agony was so sharp that her vision went white for an entire second.
’No... I won’t falter!’
Captain Kaelith lunged through the smoke.

Even half-broken by the curse she moved like a siege engine, using the dissolving smoke of Cheryl’s explosion as cover, and her greataxe swung in a wide horizontal decapitation sweep that Ther’Abella saw only because the Captain had once drilled her on that exact angle.
’I can see the attack but—’
Ther’Abella couldn’t lift her left arm.
She dropped to one knee, jammed the butt of her polearm into the mud, and caught the shaft of the greataxe with the curved crook of her silver blade.
CLAAAAAAANG!
The weight of the blow drove Ther’Abella’s knee into the stone below and shattered the joint with a sickening crunch.
"Save her," Kaelith wept with her arms straining as the green curse forced her to press the heavy axe downward toward Ther’Abella’s neck.
Ther’Abella looked into her Captain’s weeping face.
’I will.’
She let go of the polearm’s grip with her right hand, formed a rigid spear-hand with her fingers, and channeled every scrap of wind-mana she had left into a compressed high-frequency drill.
PZT!
Her hand thrust upward, piercing straight through the seam beneath Kaelith’s chin-guard and punching into the base of her skull.

Kaelith’s body stiffened as the heavy axe fell from her grip and splashed into the mud, and the green light vanished from her eyes, leaving behind only the deep gentle gray of an older sister who had watched over her since her first day on the high canopy.
"Good," Kaelith breathed, blood bubbling past her lips. "Save our Lady..."
The Captain collapsed forward with her heavy armor pinning Ther’Abella’s ruined legs to the ground.
Across the clearing, the three archers and Moriel were already advancing.
Althea nocked another arrow with shaking hands, and Moriel raised her lance, tears streaming down her cheeks as she stepped through the rain.
"AAAAAAGH!"
Ther’Abella tore her broken knee out from under Kaelith’s bulk with a violent wrench that left a trail of red behind.
She couldn’t stand as both legs were ruined, her left arm was limp, and her chest was carved with deep bleeding gashes.
’I need to move...!’
She dropped onto her stomach and, using her right elbow and her fingernails, began to claw her way forward through the mud and blood, dragging her polearm behind her by its leather strap.
THWIP!
An arrow pierced her right calf and pinned the muscle to the soil but she didn’t stop.
"U-urgh...!"
She ripped the leg forward, tearing the flesh around the shaft, and crawled inch by agonizing inch toward the Boundary Gate.
Moriel lunged with her lance whistling downward however Ther’Abella rolled onto her back and thrust her silver polearm upward with her one good arm.
SHCK!
The silver blade punched straight through Moriel’s sternum.
The spear-master gasped and collapsed over Ther’Abella’s chest, her blood spilling warm over Ther’Abella’s face.
"Thank you, little one," Moriel whispered, closing her eyes as she went limp.
Ther’Abella shoved the corpse aside and kept crawling.
The three archers dropped their bows, pulled side-daggers, and rushed forward, sobbing uncontrollably as the curse forced them to strike.
The archers did not break at all... They drew side-daggers in perfect unison and came on in a staggered line, so that whoever she struck first would leave the other two an opening.
Ther’Abella spun her polearm along the ground and swept their ankles, and in a desperate flurry of blood and mud she drove the silver blade through one throat, then another, then the third.
Splat! Splat! Splat!
All three collapsed into the grass as silence fell, broken only by the heavy drumming of the rain.
Seven corpses of the Viridian Guard lay scattered across the field with their eyes finally clear of the green curse.
"M-move... I need to move..."
She bent her broken spine and dragged her ruined body across the final twenty yards toward the Boundary Gate.
The blue light of the archway had shrunk to a narrow, flickering slit barely two feet wide.
STEP! STEP!
A pair of dark polished leather boots stepped into view and stopped directly in front of her outstretched fingers.
Slowly, with agonizing effort, she lifted her head as rain and blood dripped from her eyelashes.
Ellvi stood over her.
The usurper looked down at the broken bloody shieldmaiden with a cold mocking smile with her arms crossed beneath her heavy bust.
The stolen divine mana of the World Tree swirled around her shoulders in radiant bands of emerald light.
"Look at you," Ellvi mocked, her voice dripping with venomous amusement. "The proudest, youngest member of the Viridian Guard, crawling through her sisters’ blood like a mangled worm."
Ther’Abella bared her bloody teeth, a hoarse snarl tearing from her throat.
"You used dark magic... You cursed them to kill me..."
Ellvi threw her head back and laughed.

"Dark magic? How remarkably naive... I didn’t cast a single curse. I used one of Eluned’s own sacred spells." She tapped her temple with a polished fingernail. "It doesn’t implant anything... It simply amplifies what is already festering inside a person to its maximum... now do you know how I knew what to amplify? I spent a year reading every letter, every diary, and every private grumble your precious sisters ever wrote... Kaelith resented that you were the favorite, Caelia thought you stole her promotion, Moriel wanted your lance-training slot for her niece so each one carried a tiny, hidden seed of envy, and all I did was water them... They did the rest."
She stood back up, smoothing down her dark leather corset.
"And the citizens? They didn’t need a curse. They’ve spent a year mourning their Overlord... All they needed was someone to blame, and I handed them Eluned’s name already shaped like a verdict."
Ellvi looked down at her with pure, arrogant contempt.
"Emotions are weaknesses, Ther’Abella... Eluned spent a thousand years trying to study them like a foolish scholar and look where it got her. She’s sealed in the roots, while I wield her divinity."
She turned her gaze toward the dying slit of the Boundary Gate. It was flickering violently, shrinking to the width of a hand.

"You expected me to kill you, didn’t you?" Ellvi asked, tilting her head. "A dead traitor is only a corpse, and corpses can be argued over... A living fugitive, running into the wastes with the Overlord’s blood on her name, is a confession that walks so run, little squire. Every mile you put between yourself and Yggdrasil makes my story truer."
Ellvi drew her right leg back.
"Go... Wander the cold wastes and rot in the outer dark, knowing that you were too weak to save your Lady and too pathetic to save your sisters..."
WHAM!
Ellvi’s heavy leather boot kicked Ther’Abella squarely in the ribs as the impact lifted Ther’Abella’s mangled frame into the air and hurled her through the closing aperture of the portal.
’N-no,’ Ther’Abella thought.

She reached out with her bloody, trembling fingers, trying desperately to claw at the stone edge of the gate and pull herself back toward the World Tree, toward the library, toward Lady Eluned’s gentle face.
’LADY ELUNED!’
SNAP!
The gate collapsed inward as the blue light died into nothingness, and the world turned pitch-black.
Ther’Abella fell.
There was no wind to whistle in her ears, no sound of rushing sky... it was only the agonizing phantom drag of momentum through the collapsed threshold.
In the pitch-black silence, the world refused to remain quiet.
Her memories began to bleed backward into the dark.
She heard them.
...Laughter.

It was the bright, ringing chime of Caelia’s giggles over a pitcher of fermented pear juice, the deep exasperated chuckle of Captain Kaelith as she dropped a training schedule onto the cedar desk, the quiet, teasing murmur of Moriel as she adjusted the grip on Ther’Abella’s very first lance.
They had shared the same hearth beneath the bough... They had bandaged one another’s blisters, broken bread under the canopy, and sworn their breaths to the same living sovereign...
’...They were always envious of me.’
The realization hit her not with fury but with a dull hollow ache that felt far worse than the shattered bones in her chest.
Ellvi’s poisoned words rang through the darkness, she didn’t invent it... she only amplified what was already festering.
It made no sense to her aching mind. She had looked up to every single one of them.

She had believed, with the earnest simplicity of a younger sister, that their circle was an unshakeable fortress yet beneath the smiles, beneath the affectionate ruffling of her silver hair and the shared cups of spring tea, a quiet bitter seed had been taking root.
They had looked at the way Lady Eluned smiled in the library, at the gentle rare warmth the Goddess reserved for her youngest squire, and they had swallowed down venom.
And in the end, it took so little to bring it to the surface... Just a whisper.
’And Lady Eluned.’
A suffocating knot seized her throat.
’I failed her.’
She had let the Lady be dragged down into the roots.
She had stood by while the heartwood split open and the lightless chasm swallowed that small green-clad figure whole.

The gentle, untouchable goddess who had wondered aloud what it meant to fall in love, who had dreamed of little footsteps on wooden floorboards and peaceful evenings beneath the orchard, was now entombed in the suffocating black, branded as a murderer by the very people she had nurtured.
Ther’Abella’s fingers twitched against the void.
’I couldn’t save the guard... I couldn’t save my Lady...’
She swallowed.
’...I couldn’t even die beside them.’

She was fighting the finest squad in the Sovereign Realm, and every one of them was still fighting well...
If she didn’t fight, she would die here and if she died here, no one would ever know the truth.
’This...’
Lady Eluned would remain trapped in that dark suffocating chasm for eternity, remembered as a traitor who had killed someone she had viewed as her own brother.
’Forgive me.’
Ther’Abella planted her left hand in the mud and channeled her wind-mana.
FWOOM!
A concussive shockwave erupted from her palm, blasting the mud outward and jarring the twins’ balance for half a second.
In that tiny opening, she pivoted on her good knee and swung her silver polearm in a horizontal arc.
The blade caught Caelia across the chest, carved through her leather cuirass, and sliced deep into her lungs.
Before Evandra could scream, Ther’Abella used the rotational momentum of the swing to drive the iron-capped butt of the weapon upward into Evandra’s chin.
CRACK!
Evandra’s neck snapped backward and both sisters collapsed into the mud with their blood mingling in the cold puddle.
As the green light faded from Caelia’s dying eyes, she looked up through the rain.
"Thank you," Caelia whispered, her breath rattling out in a final quiet sigh.
Evandra’s hand twitched once against her sister’s sleeve, and then both went still.
THWIP-THWIP-THWIP!
Three explosive arrows tore through the downpour.
One punched through Ther’Abella’s left bicep, detonating on exit and tearing the muscle from the bone and the agony was so sharp that her vision went white for an entire second.
I won’t falter!’
Captain Kaelith lunged through the smoke.

Even half-broken by the curse she moved like a siege engine, using the dissolving smoke of Cheryl’s explosion as cover, and her greataxe swung in a wide horizontal decapitation sweep that Ther’Abella saw only because the Captain had once drilled her on that exact angle.
’I can see the attack but—’
Ther’Abella couldn’t lift her left arm.
She dropped to one knee, jammed the butt of her polearm into the mud, and caught the shaft of the greataxe with the curved crook of her silver blade.
CLAAAAAAANG!
The weight of the blow drove Ther’Abella’s knee into the stone below and shattered the joint with a sickening crunch.
"Save her," Kaelith wept with her arms straining as the green curse forced her to press the heavy axe downward toward Ther’Abella’s neck.
Ther’Abella looked into her Captain’s weeping face.
’I will.’
She let go of the polearm’s grip with her right hand, formed a rigid spear-hand with her fingers, and channeled every scrap of wind-mana she had left into a compressed high-frequency drill.
PZT!
Her hand thrust upward, piercing straight through the seam beneath Kaelith’s chin-guard and punching into the base of her skull.

Kaelith’s body stiffened as the heavy axe fell from her grip and splashed into the mud, and the green light vanished from her eyes, leaving behind only the deep gentle gray of an older sister who had watched over her since her first day on the high canopy.
"Good," Kaelith breathed, blood bubbling past her lips.
"Save our Lady..."
The Captain collapsed forward with her heavy armor pinning Ther’Abella’s ruined legs to the ground.
Across the clearing, the three archers and Moriel were already advancing.
Althea nocked another arrow with shaking hands, and Moriel raised her lance, tears streaming down her cheeks as she stepped through the rain.
"AAAAAAGH!"
Ther’Abella tore her broken knee out from under Kaelith’s bulk with a violent wrench that left a trail of red behind.
She couldn’t stand as both legs were ruined, her left arm was limp, and her chest was carved with deep bleeding gashes.
’I need to move...!’
She dropped onto her stomach and, using her right elbow and her fingernails, began to claw her way forward through the mud and blood, dragging her polearm behind her by its leather strap.
THWIP!
An arrow pierced her right calf and pinned the muscle to the soil but she didn’t stop.
"U-urgh...!"
She ripped the leg forward, tearing the flesh around the shaft, and crawled inch by agonizing inch toward the Boundary Gate.
Moriel lunged with her lance whistling downward however Ther’Abella rolled onto her back and thrust her silver polearm upward with her one good arm.
SHCK!
The silver blade punched straight through Moriel’s sternum.
The spear-master gasped and collapsed over Ther’Abella’s chest, her blood spilling warm over Ther’Abella’s face.
"Thank you, little one," Moriel whispered, closing her eyes as she went limp.
Ther’Abella shoved the corpse aside and kept crawling.
The three archers dropped their bows, pulled side-daggers, and rushed forward, sobbing uncontrollably as the curse forced them to strike.
The archers did not break at all...
They drew side-daggers in perfect unison and came on in a staggered line, so that whoever she struck first would leave the other two an opening.
Ther’Abella spun her polearm along the ground and swept their ankles, and in a desperate flurry of blood and mud she drove the silver blade through one throat, then another, then the third.
Splat!
Splat!
Splat!
All three collapsed into the grass as silence fell, broken only by the heavy drumming of the rain.
Seven corpses of the Viridian Guard lay scattered across the field with their eyes finally clear of the green curse.
"M-move...
I need to move..."
She bent her broken spine and dragged her ruined body across the final twenty yards toward the Boundary Gate.
The blue light of the archway had shrunk to a narrow, flickering slit barely two feet wide.
STEP!
STEP!
A pair of dark polished leather boots stepped into view and stopped directly in front of her outstretched fingers.
Slowly, with agonizing effort, she lifted her head as rain and blood dripped from her eyelashes.
Ellvi stood over her.
The usurper looked down at the broken bloody shieldmaiden with a cold mocking smile with her arms crossed beneath her heavy bust.
The stolen divine mana of the World Tree swirled around her shoulders in radiant bands of emerald light.
"Look at you," Ellvi mocked, her voice dripping with venomous amusement.
"The proudest, youngest member of the Viridian Guard, crawling through her sisters’ blood like a mangled worm."
Ther’Abella bared her bloody teeth, a hoarse snarl tearing from her throat.
"You used dark magic...
You cursed them to kill me..."
Ellvi threw her head back and laughed.
"Dark magic?
How remarkably naive...
I didn’t cast a single curse.
I used one of Eluned’s own sacred spells." She tapped her temple with a polished fingernail.
"It doesn’t implant anything...
It simply amplifies what is already festering inside a person to its maximum... now do you know how I knew what to amplify?
I spent a year reading every letter, every diary, and every private grumble your precious sisters ever wrote...

Kaelith resented that you were the favorite, Caelia thought you stole her promotion, Moriel wanted your lance-training slot for her niece so each one carried a tiny, hidden seed of envy, and all I did was water them...
They did the rest."
She stood back up, smoothing down her dark leather corset.
"And the citizens?
They didn’t need a curse.
They’ve spent a year mourning their Overlord...
All they needed was someone to blame, and I handed them Eluned’s name already shaped like a verdict."
Ellvi looked down at her with pure, arrogant contempt.
"Emotions are weaknesses, Ther’Abella...
Eluned spent a thousand years trying to study them like a foolish scholar and look where it got her.
She’s sealed in the roots, while I wield her divinity."
She turned her gaze toward the dying slit of the Boundary Gate.
It was flickering violently, shrinking to the width of a hand.
"You expected me to kill you, didn’t you?" Ellvi asked, tilting her head.
"A dead traitor is only a corpse, and corpses can be argued over...
A living fugitive, running into the wastes with the Overlord’s blood on her name, is a confession that walks so run, little squire.
Every mile you put between yourself and Yggdrasil makes my story truer."
Ellvi drew her right leg back.
Wander the cold wastes and rot in the outer dark, knowing that you were too weak to save your Lady and too pathetic to save your sisters..."
WHAM!
Ellvi’s heavy leather boot kicked Ther’Abella squarely in the ribs as the impact lifted Ther’Abella’s mangled frame into the air and hurled her through the closing aperture of the portal.
’N-no,’ Ther’Abella thought.

She reached out with her bloody, trembling fingers, trying desperately to claw at the stone edge of the gate and pull herself back toward the World Tree, toward the library, toward Lady Eluned’s gentle face.
’LADY ELUNED!’
SNAP!
The gate collapsed inward as the blue light died into nothingness, and the world turned pitch-black.
Ther’Abella fell.
There was no wind to whistle in her ears, no sound of rushing sky... it was only the agonizing phantom drag of momentum through the collapsed threshold.
In the pitch-black silence, the world refused to remain quiet.
Her memories began to bleed backward into the dark.
She heard them.
...Laughter.

It was the bright, ringing chime of Caelia’s giggles over a pitcher of fermented pear juice, the deep exasperated chuckle of Captain Kaelith as she dropped a training schedule onto the cedar desk, the quiet, teasing murmur of Moriel as she adjusted the grip on Ther’Abella’s very first lance.
They had shared the same hearth beneath the bough...
They had bandaged one another’s blisters, broken bread under the canopy, and sworn their breaths to the same living sovereign...
’...They were always envious of me.’
The realization hit her not with fury but with a dull hollow ache that felt far worse than the shattered bones in her chest.
Ellvi’s poisoned words rang through the darkness, she didn’t invent it... she only amplified what was already festering.
It made no sense to her aching mind.
She had looked up to every single one of them.

She had believed, with the earnest simplicity of a younger sister, that their circle was an unshakeable fortress yet beneath the smiles, beneath the affectionate ruffling of her silver hair and the shared cups of spring tea, a quiet bitter seed had been taking root.
They had looked at the way Lady Eluned smiled in the library, at the gentle rare warmth the Goddess reserved for her youngest squire, and they had swallowed down venom.
And in the end, it took so little to bring it to the surface...
Just a whisper.
’And Lady Eluned.’
A suffocating knot seized her throat.
’I failed her.’
She had let the Lady be dragged down into the roots.
She had stood by while the heartwood split open and the lightless chasm swallowed that small green-clad figure whole.

The gentle, untouchable goddess who had wondered aloud what it meant to fall in love, who had dreamed of little footsteps on wooden floorboards and peaceful evenings beneath the orchard, was now entombed in the suffocating black, branded as a murderer by the very people she had nurtured.
Ther’Abella’s fingers twitched against the void.
’I couldn’t save the guard...
I couldn’t save my Lady...’
She swallowed.
’...I couldn’t even die beside them.’

chapters.title: Chapter 650: Ther’Abella, The Wandering Soul
paragraphs: The descent abruptly seized as the weightless drop vanished, replaced by the bone-crushing jolt of her mangled spine striking solid ground.
BOOM!
The breath exploded from her lungs in a wet gasp, spraying dark crimson across coarse dust.
She lay there, half-buried in dry earth with every nerve ending screaming in white-hot agony.
The dark above her was no longer a dimensional rift.
It was an open foreign sky that looked flat and utterly indifferent.
"I... I really want to die."
Her eyelids fluttered shut with her pulse slowing to a weak irregular crawl... Right now...
To close her eyes and let the dust settle over her face felt so easy, it felt like the only merciful thing left in the world.
’Get up.’
The voice echoed inside her skull... the voice kept on saying it over and over again, it was annoying... why was it so annoying? Who owned that—
...It was her own voice.
’GET UP!’
Ther’Abella’s eyes snapped wide.
SKRRRRR-SNAP!
A shadow fell over her face, carrying the foul sulfurous stench of rot and saliva.
Looming directly above her was a silhouette was a desert stalker with mottled sand-colored chitin and four unblinking milky eyes.
Its mandible was parted wide, revealing rows of translucent serrated fangs dripping with digestive acid, lunging straight down to bite off her skull.
Her body had no strength to roll. Her left arm hung limp, and her legs were useless ribbons of ruined muscle.
’Move!’
With a feral scream that tore her throat raw, Ther’Abella reached into the bottom of her withered core.

The microscopic dregs of her wind-mana flared into life and hissed along the cracked pathways of her right arm as she thrust her open palm straight into the beast’s descending maw, and a needle of compressed air detonated inside the creature’s palate.
BANG!
The shockwave blew the top of the monster’s skull apart in a spray of thick greenish-black ichor and shattered carapace.
The heavy twitching carcass collapsed over her legs, its limbs spasming in the sand before going limp.
"Haah... Haah... Haah..."
Panting heavily, her vision swimming with dark spots, Ther’Abella shoved the dead weight off her knees with the heel of her hand.
Silence rushed back in as she lay flat on her back, drawing in short shallow drafts of air that tasted of dry salt and baked earth, and looked around.
There were no emerald leaves and there were no clean singing springs either.
As far as the horizon stretched beneath the pale, washed-out sky, there was only a desolate wind-swept expanse of gray dunes, jagged stone ridges, and cracked barren flats.
The air was dry and scorching and carried none of the rich vitality that had nourished her soul since her birth.
’A desert,’ she thought, her lips cracking as she swallowed. ’An outer zone...’
She turned her senses inward to assess the damage.
Her spiritual circuits were scorched, their walls paper-thin and trembling from the violent spatial expulsion.
Her mana pool, once a deep reservoir that could fuel days of high-speed maneuvers, was practically hollowed out.
She closed her eyes, bit down on her tongue to focus through the pain, and began to weave what little mana she possessed.
A pale-green thread of restorative energy crawled slowly across her fractured bones.
"I’m going to survive..."
It took agonizing minutes just to set the alignment of her left arm, and the bone knitted with a slow grinding ache.
Next came her shattered kneecap, which she dragged together just enough to support her weight.
She could not afford to heal the lacerations on her ribs or the deep gouges along her thighs.
Every drop of mana spent on flesh was ether she wouldn’t have if another scavenger crossed the ridge.
By the time the green light sputtered and died, the sun was sinking, casting long bleeding crimson shadows across the dunes and she was alive... barely.
Ther’Abella reached to her side, and her dirt-caked fingers wrapped around the familiar leather grip of her silver-bladed polearm.
The metal was chipped and smeared with dried blood that was not her own, but the shaft remained unyielding.

She drove the iron butt of the weapon into the hard-packed sand and, with a low groan, forced her trembling legs beneath her, leaning her full weight against the polearm until she stood upright under the alien sky.
She looked north.
...It was just sand.
She looked south.
...It was endless barren stone.
Behind her, the path back to the World Tree was gone, collapsed into the void by the hands of a traitor.
Ahead lay an untamed lawless wilderness where ancient entities and ruthless people carved their domains from the marrow of the weak.
She had no home, she had no sisters and she had no Lady to answer her morning salute.
The elf was an unclaimed weapon left behind in the dust.
Ther’Abella raised her chin with her long silver hair whipping across her face in the rising desert wind.
She lifted her blade, wiped the sand from the steel with the torn hem of her sleeve, and did the one thing she knew how to do...
Ther’Abella began to wander.
The desert had no seasons... It had daylight that cracked the skin and nights that froze the spit in a traveler’s mouth...
In the first year she learned which lizards could be eaten raw and which would turn her bowels to water.
She learned to drink the dew from a corpse’s ribs at dawn and to sleep standing up, leaning on her polearm like a scarecrow, because anything that lay down in the Calcid Basin did not get up again.
Her boots wore down to thin leather, then to raw cord, then to bandages stripped from the hides of dune stalkers and bound tight with dried sinew.

Ther’Abella notched each day into the shaft of her polearm until the wood became a field of tiny wounds, and somewhere past thirty thousand notches she stopped counting because the number no longer meant anything... she would be here for a log time.
A century passed in a blur of dust and severed meat.
When a three-headed sand-drake reared from the dunes of the Calcid Basin, its throat swelling with liquid copper, she did not bother weaving defensive spells as she would have done.
The first head spat, and the molten spray hissed across the sand where she had stood a heartbeat earlier.
She ducked beneath the sweep of its lateral horn, planted her left heel into the shifting grit, and rammed the butt of her polearm upward into its soft lower jaw.
The beast bucked, and she rode the recoil, twisting through the air like a spinning leaf.
The crescent blade came down in a single vertical cleave that sheared through the central cervical vertebrae and the two remaining heads screamed in unison before the body fell.
Black blood hissed against the hot sand.
She landed, wiped the edge against the creature’s flank, and kept walking before the carcass had finished twitching.
’I’ve become stronger...’
In the second century she tried to go home.

She crossed the Glass Wastes, where an ancient sun-flare had fused the desert into mirrors that burned her eyes through closed lids, and she followed a dimming memory of the road the Guard had patrolled in the first year of her service.
She found the place where the Outer Boundary Gate should have stood.
There was only a scar of petrified root and a ring of dead blue crystal, and above it a ward of cold green light that hummed with a familiar signature.
...It would not let her within a mile.
She stood in front of that shimmering place for three days.
On the fourth, a merchant caravan passed along the old road, and she listened from behind a rock as the drovers laughed around their fire and sang.
It was a ballad about the Elven Overlord.
It had a second verse about the Betrayer of the Roots, the Goddess who had murdered her own brother with dark magic and was buried alive for it, and a chorus that rhymed her name with a curse.
The drovers all knew the words... They were children’s words, the kind that would be taught to the next generation, and the generation after... but she did not draw her blade.
She walked into the Glass Wastes and kept walking until the song was too far away to hear, and then she walked a few miles more, just to be sure.
Her wind-mana, once clear and sweet like the mountain boughs of Yggdrasil, began to curdle and freeze in the endless dry void.

She felt it go, the way a tooth goes loose before it comes out and in the deep salt caverns beneath the Black Scarp, cornered by a swarm of blind chittering carapace-crawlers, her lungs seized from sulfur inhalation.

The tunnel behind her was collapsed and the tunnel ahead was a river of carapace and clicking mandibles... She was going to die in the dark, and her last coherent thought was that she had not even cried out for the Lady.

So she stopped reaching for the absent life-force of the great bough as her spiritual pathways tore themselves open out of rabid desperation, and she reached upward, past the cavern roof, past the cracked ceiling of the realm, dragging down the cold unfeeling glare of dead constellations.
The air inverted.
Her eyes burned with cold violet fire as delicate stellar markings, fine cosmic constellations, etched themselves permanently across her high cheekbones like silver scars.

With a flick of her wrists, the silver polearm in her grip dissolved into a concentrated needle of white starlight, and when she swept it across the dark forty chitinous horrors were cut in half without making a sound with their vitals cauterized by the freezing heat of dying suns.
Ther’Abella stood in the silence afterward with steam rising from the cooling stone as she discovered that she was no longer afraid of the dark.
The third century was a blur of necessity.
Combat stopped being a discipline.
It stopped being an art she had practiced with Captain Kaelith on the green terraces while the others giggled over tea... It became an unthinking reflex as basic as chewing or blinking.
She swung, something broke, and she stepped over the mess.

Her shoulders broadened under the weight of it, her forearms hardened into cords of lean muscle, and she grew into the tall hard-edged warrior frame of a creature that had never once been allowed to rest.
Her level climbed past two hundred, past three, past four too...
She killed wardens of dead kingdoms and rift-beasts the size of cathedrals.
She killed warlords who tried to press her into service and bandit kings who tried to rob her.

When a famine-wraith took the oasis town of Sedgerun by the throat, she walked into its fog alone and walked out the next morning with its antlered skull on her shoulder and eight hundred villagers alive behind her.
They tried to give her gold, a cottage, and a bride-price in saffron but she would not take any of it.
At Ashgate, a warlord who called himself the Iron Sovereign met her at the head of nine thousand men and offered her a captaincy, a harem, and half his plunder.
She asked him a single question, whether he had ever kept a vow, and when he laughed she walked down the line of his champions one at a time.
The first fell to the flat of her blade and the second discovered that a starlight lance cannot be parried while the third dropped his weapon before she reached him.
By the time she stood in front of the Sovereign himself, the nine thousand had sat down on the sand, one rank after another, as though somebody had cut their strings but she did not kill him.
She took the war-banner from his tent, cut it into bandages, and left them on the doorstep of the nearest healer’s hut with no note.

On clear nights she lay on her back and traced the constellations etched on her own cheeks in the dark. She had learned their names from a drunken astronomer in a ruined observatory who died two days later in his sleep with a smile on his face and her cloak laid over him.
The elf could not be thanked... Gratitude was a leash, and every leash she remembered ended at a knife...
Every dawn she did one thing that had nothing to do with survival.
She planted the butt of her polearm in the sand, turned toward a horizon that held no tree, and brought her right fist across her collarbone in the salute of the Viridian Guard.
"Good morning, Lady," she would say to the empty light.
Then she waited, the way she used to wait on the green terrace for the small calm voice to answer, and when no answer came she lowered her hand and went to kill something.
...She did it for four hundred years without missing a morning, and it never once got easier.
Centuries bled into four hundred years.

Across the outer fringes of the Sovereign Realm, past the lawless free-zones, the mercenary camps, and the trading posts where exiled vagrants bartered scrap iron and void-pelts, whispers gathered like blowing grit.
They called her The Wanderer.
They spoke of a tall, silver-haired elf with sunken bloodshot eyes that burned with lilac starlight when she drew steel.
She carried no house crest and she wore no sovereign sigil either.
She butchered Tier 4 abominations and roaming warlords alike if they crossed her path, but she never claimed territory and never spoke two words where one would do.

"She’s a mad dog," the caravan masters would mutter over their campfires. "She’ll step between an iron-boar and an orphan without batting an eye, but try to hand her a gold coin to say thanks, and she’ll look at you like you’re dung beneath her boot..."
On the first night of the four-hundred-and-first year, the evening gale carried the smell of baked clay and old pipe smoke to the lip of the Southern Ridge.
Ther’Abella crested the last dune and saw, below her, the crooked lantern-lit shape of a frontier outpost.
It had a well, a corral, and a tavern with a wooden sign that swung on rusted hinges and read... [THE SAND-SKIMMER’S REST]
She looked at the lights for a long moment then she started down the slope.

...It would not let her within a mile.
She stood in front of that shimmering place for three days.
On the fourth, a merchant caravan passed along the old road, and she listened from behind a rock as the drovers laughed around their fire and sang.
It was a ballad about the Elven Overlord.
It had a second verse about the Betrayer of the Roots, the Goddess who had murdered her own brother with dark magic and was buried alive for it, and a chorus that rhymed her name with a curse.
The drovers all knew the words...
They were children’s words, the kind that would be taught to the next generation, and the generation after... but she did not draw her blade.
She walked into the Glass Wastes and kept walking until the song was too far away to hear, and then she walked a few miles more, just to be sure.
Her wind-mana, once clear and sweet like the mountain boughs of Yggdrasil, began to curdle and freeze in the endless dry void.

She felt it go, the way a tooth goes loose before it comes out and in the deep salt caverns beneath the Black Scarp, cornered by a swarm of blind chittering carapace-crawlers, her lungs seized from sulfur inhalation.
The tunnel behind her was collapsed and the tunnel ahead was a river of carapace and clicking mandibles...
She was going to die in the dark, and her last coherent thought was that she had not even cried out for the Lady.

So she stopped reaching for the absent life-force of the great bough as her spiritual pathways tore themselves open out of rabid desperation, and she reached upward, past the cavern roof, past the cracked ceiling of the realm, dragging down the cold unfeeling glare of dead constellations.
The air inverted.
Her eyes burned with cold violet fire as delicate stellar markings, fine cosmic constellations, etched themselves permanently across her high cheekbones like silver scars.

With a flick of her wrists, the silver polearm in her grip dissolved into a concentrated needle of white starlight, and when she swept it across the dark forty chitinous horrors were cut in half without making a sound with their vitals cauterized by the freezing heat of dying suns.
Ther’Abella stood in the silence afterward with steam rising from the cooling stone as she discovered that she was no longer afraid of the dark.
The third century was a blur of necessity.
Combat stopped being a discipline.
It stopped being an art she had practiced with Captain Kaelith on the green terraces while the others giggled over tea...
It became an unthinking reflex as basic as chewing or blinking.
She swung, something broke, and she stepped over the mess.

Her shoulders broadened under the weight of it, her forearms hardened into cords of lean muscle, and she grew into the tall hard-edged warrior frame of a creature that had never once been allowed to rest.
Her level climbed past two hundred, past three, past four too...
She killed wardens of dead kingdoms and rift-beasts the size of cathedrals.
She killed warlords who tried to press her into service and bandit kings who tried to rob her.

When a famine-wraith took the oasis town of Sedgerun by the throat, she walked into its fog alone and walked out the next morning with its antlered skull on her shoulder and eight hundred villagers alive behind her.
They tried to give her gold, a cottage, and a bride-price in saffron but she would not take any of it.
At Ashgate, a warlord who called himself the Iron Sovereign met her at the head of nine thousand men and offered her a captaincy, a harem, and half his plunder.
She asked him a single question, whether he had ever kept a vow, and when he laughed she walked down the line of his champions one at a time.
The first fell to the flat of her blade and the second discovered that a starlight lance cannot be parried while the third dropped his weapon before she reached him.
By the time she stood in front of the Sovereign himself, the nine thousand had sat down on the sand, one rank after another, as though somebody had cut their strings but she did not kill him.
She took the war-banner from his tent, cut it into bandages, and left them on the doorstep of the nearest healer’s hut with no note.
On clear nights she lay on her back and traced the constellations etched on her own cheeks in the dark.
She had learned their names from a drunken astronomer in a ruined observatory who died two days later in his sleep with a smile on his face and her cloak laid over him.
The elf could not be thanked...
Gratitude was a leash, and every leash she remembered ended at a knife...
Every dawn she did one thing that had nothing to do with survival.
She planted the butt of her polearm in the sand, turned toward a horizon that held no tree, and brought her right fist across her collarbone in the salute of the Viridian Guard.
"Good morning, Lady," she would say to the empty light.
Then she waited, the way she used to wait on the green terrace for the small calm voice to answer, and when no answer came she lowered her hand and went to kill something.
...She did it for four hundred years without missing a morning, and it never once got easier.
Centuries bled into four hundred years.

Across the outer fringes of the Sovereign Realm, past the lawless free-zones, the mercenary camps, and the trading posts where exiled vagrants bartered scrap iron and void-pelts, whispers gathered like blowing grit.
They called her The Wanderer.
They spoke of a tall, silver-haired elf with sunken bloodshot eyes that burned with lilac starlight when she drew steel.
She carried no house crest and she wore no sovereign sigil either.
She butchered Tier 4 abominations and roaming warlords alike if they crossed her path, but she never claimed territory and never spoke two words where one would do.
"She’s a mad dog," the caravan masters would mutter over their campfires.
"She’ll step between an iron-boar and an orphan without batting an eye, but try to hand her a gold coin to say thanks, and she’ll look at you like you’re dung beneath her boot..."
On the first night of the four-hundred-and-first year, the evening gale carried the smell of baked clay and old pipe smoke to the lip of the Southern Ridge.
Ther’Abella crested the last dune and saw, below her, the crooked lantern-lit shape of a frontier outpost.
It had a well, a corral, and a tavern with a wooden sign that swung on rusted hinges and read...
[THE SAND-SKIMMER’S REST]
She looked at the lights for a long moment then she started down the slope.

chapters.title: Chapter 651: A Wish And The World’s Reply
paragraphs: The tavern was loud and smelled of stale barley mash as well as weed.
Mercenaries, low-tier Awakened prospectors, and caravan guards sat crammed elbow-to-elbow along the pine benches, shouting over dice and slamming wooden tankards against the tables.
CREAK!
The heavy sand-scoured oak door swung open.
’I really dislike this place...’
The tavern did not quiet at once, but a cold sharp drop in atmospheric pressure rolled through the doorway like an icy draft.
A tall figure stepped across the threshold, ducking her chin to clear the low beam.

Her silver hair hung in frayed uneven locks past her shoulder blades, caked in white dust and her traveler’s cloak was shredded at the hem, pinned over a tarnished cuirass that had lost its polish three centuries ago while the forearms that emerged from its torn sleeves were corded with lean hard muscle, crossed with old white scars.

The delicate stellar markings on her pale cheekbones caught the dim lantern light while her piercing blue eyes, rimmed with an exhausted bloodshot look swept the room with the flat indifference of a reaper checking its victims.
The noise in the tavern died by half.
Drunk mercenaries froze with tankards halfway to their lips.
Men who had been boasting about hunting desert hyenas leaned back and slid their daggers further under the benches.
A dice game stopped mid-throw, and somebody’s cup rolled off a table and landed with a hollow clatter nobody dared to pick up.
Four men by the hearth did not freeze with the others.
They wore the gray scarves of a bounty guild, and the biggest of them had a rolled parchment tucked into his belt, with a smudged charcoal sketch of silver hair.
He stood, loosening a chain-flail from his hip.
"That’s her... Twelve thousand credits for the head."
Ther’Abella did not break stride.
She turned her head the barest fraction of an inch, and the starlight in her eyes flared once in a brief cold lilac that lit every face in the room.
The big man’s flail slid from his fingers and rang on the floorboards as the other three sat back down.
It was not simply a threat... It was a verdict, delivered so quietly that the barkeep, who had seen three brawls a week for twenty years, could swear that he hadn’t seen her do anything at all.
Ther’Abella ignored them all.
She walked straight to the wooden counter with her boots making a dry scuffing scrape against the floorboards, and rested two calloused fingers against the scarred wood.
"A room," She said and her voice was raspy as unwatered gravel. "A washbasin. Key."
The tavern owner, a balding middle-aged man with thick forearms and an apron stained with grease, stared at her.
His eyes went wide as saucers, dropping to her scarred polearm, then darting to the constellations on her face.

"Y-You," he stammered, and dropped the rag he was holding, nearly knocking over a row of pewter mugs as he stumbled around the counter. "You’re her! The silver woman from the Southern Ridge! Three weeks ago my daughter, Mara, was leading an escort wagon through the dunes when a pack of sand-crawlers hit them... You slaughtered the whole brood and dragged her cart out of the pit!"
"Key," Ther’Abella said.

"Please, My Lady!" the man pleaded, tears welling in his red eyes as he fumbled beneath the till, dragging out a heavy iron key with both hands. "Stay as long as you wish! A month! A year! The top suite, clean sheets, a private cistern, anything! Let me roast a flank of mountain goat for you! Mara has been wanting to thank you... If you could only sign your name on her guild token, she would cherish it forever!"
Ther’Abella took the iron key from his palm before his fingers could close but she did not look at him.
She did not look at the meat skewers roasting over the hearth, even though her stomach turned over once at the smell.
She turned on her heel and started toward the narrow wooden staircase with her shoulders hunched beneath the torn cloak.
"Hey!" a drunken brawler at a corner table sneered, slamming his fist onto the pine. "The barkeep is offering you free meat, you stuck-up pointy-eared bitch! You can’t even say thank you?!"
Ther’Abella did not stop.
She walked up the stairs, each heavy step creaking under her weight, and disappeared into the dark corridor above.
"Rude bastard," someone grumbled into his ale down below. "Save your life and she treats you like dirt on her heel... Let her rot in the desert..."
CLICK!
She turned the iron key in the lock, shoved the warped pine door open, and stepped inside.
The room was small, containing a low cot with a scratchy wool blanket, a three-legged wooden stool, and a cracked ceramic basin filled with lukewarm yellow-tinted well water.

She dropped her polearm against the wall, and the metal clattered against the plaster with a heavy dead thud then she walked to the basin, leaned over it, gripping the chipped porcelain rim until her knuckles went white, and stared down into the cloudy water.
Her reflection stared back.
She had a pale hollow face, with dark purple bags hanging beneath bloodshot eyes.
The silver constellations along her cheekbones looked like scars left by an iron brand.
The ancient viridian-woven fabric beneath her cloak was shredded and caked in the dried fluids of a thousand dead monsters.
"Disgrace," she croaked into the empty room.
The hands in the water were not the hands of the girl who had once been afraid of resin vats.
They were wide-knuckled and scarred, with calluses she could have struck sparks from.
She plunged them in and splashed her face with rough aggressive strokes.
SPLASH! SPLASH!
The cold stung her chapped lips and the cuts along her temple, but she did not stop.
She scrubbed at her skin as though she could scour away the grit, the blood, and the four hundred years that clung to her pores like grease.
When she lifted her dripping face, the cracked mirror on the wall showed the same stranger.
"Four hundred years," she whispered to the glass with her breath hitching. "And what have you done, Ther’Abella? What have you accomplished?"
...Nothing.
She had not saved her Lady... She had not avenged her Guard... She had not even managed to be kind to the people who tried to be kind to her...
If a record existed, it would be quite empty.

She had killed beasts... She had swung her blade until her wrists went numb and her muscles burned like hot wire... She had accumulated skills, refined her starlight to a lethal razor’s edge, and pushed her level to heights that ordinary elves could only dream of and for what?
’Lady Eluned.’
The name carved through her thoughts like a rusted saw.
Time within Yggdrasil moved faster than the wastes.
An hour in the wastes could stretch into days upon the great bough, and stripped of her divine mantle, how long could Eluned survive?
Ellvi had taken the core.

What if four centuries out here had been millennia in the roots? What if Lady Eluned was already dead, reduced to petrified ash in that lightless chasm while Ther’Abella scrubbed dirt off her chin in a two-bit desert tavern?
’If I go to Yggdrasil,’ she thought with water dripping from her silver bangs onto the floorboards, ’all I will do is get myself killed.’
The bitter shameful truth tasted like bile in her throat. She was afraid of dying.

...Not because she valued this miserable dust-choked existence, since she would have slit her own throat four centuries ago if it meant paying for her failure, but because she was afraid of dying before she reached the roots.
If she fell to Ellvi’s guards at the gate, no one would ever know the truth.
The world would forever remember Eluned as a fratricidal monster and friends? Comrades?
A shudder ran through her shoulders. Every time an adventurer tried to speak to her, every time a mercenary offered to share a watch, her mind flashed back to the rain-slick causeway.

To Captain Kaelith crying while she swung a greataxe... To Caelia and Evandra sobbing while their scimitars carved through her flesh... Ellvi’s poisoned words had burned themselves into her marrow... All I did was amplify what was already there.
...She could not trust anyone.
If her own sisters, the women who had braided her hair and sworn their lives to the same bough, had harbored that kind of lethal envy beneath their smiles, what would a stranger do?
Ther’Abella turned away from the mirror with her legs trembling, and collapsed onto the thin mattress, staring blankly up at the water-stained cedar rafters.
She reached into her tattered belt pouch and turned it upside down.
Clink!
A single worn copper coin rolled onto the rough blanket, followed by a pinch of dried salt.

That was her entire earthly wealth after four centuries of warfare... She had given away every pelt, tossed every reward pouch back into the dirt, and walked away from every merchant who tried to pay her.
A woman who refused to take a single scrap, left with an empty pocket in a rat-infested room.
She stared at the copper coin, and a humorless chuckle rattled in her chest.
"Right," she murmured to the dark ceiling. "Today is my birthday."
Every year on this day, the Guard had pretended to forget.

Evandra would announce that the third rotation needed extra drills, Captain Kaelith would assign her the resin vats, and Moriel would "accidentally" leave the training yard gate open so that Ther’Abella took the long way around.
And every year, when she finally dragged herself back to the barracks at midnight, there was a single white star-lotus pressed on her pillow, its petals still wet with dew, with no note and no name.
She had known whose hand had left it, and Lady Eluned had known that she knew but neither of them had ever mentioned it.
She closed her eyes, letting her head sink into the lumpy straw pillow.
Her mind drifted back to the quiet library, to the smell of blooming star-lotuses, to a green-clad Goddess pouting over a romance novel and wondering what it felt like to love someone.

’I have a wish,’ Ther’Abella thought, her hands folding over her torn tunic. ’Whatever deity is listening, whatever higher power watches over this miserable broken realm, I don’t care about my life... I don’t care about my soul... Just please... Reunite me with Lady Eluned...’
DING!
Ther’Abella’s eyes snapped wide.
Floating in the empty air three inches before her nose was a pale, translucent interface glowing with a cold blue light.
[You have been summoned to be a Hero for a Lord.]
[Accept the tether? Y / N]
She sat bolt upright on the cot, her breath catching.
"A Hero summoning," she whispered, her brow furrowing in deep suspicion.
A trick.
...It had to be a trick.
Another cruel hallucination, or a trap woven by the same hands that had hunted her through four centuries of silence.
She knew the laws well.
When an Awakened Lord established a domain, they burned tickets at an altar to pull wandering souls or dimensional remnants into their roster.
To become a summoned Hero meant binding yourself to a territory’s central stone.

’If I become part of a territory,’ she thought with her mind racing. ’A proper lord’s domain provides buffs, resource arrays, fast-travel corridors, and mana springs... The speed at which a summoned Hero can accumulate combat stats is tenfold compared to a wild wanderer.’
She needed power... Real catastrophic power, if she was ever going to break through Yggdrasil and tear Ellvi’s throat out.
Her finger rose, hovering over the glowing letter as she tapped [ Y ].
HUMMMMMMMM.
The interface shifted instantly with text flashing in stark warning crimson.
[Your level will be forcefully reset from Level 555 → Level 1. You will lose some of your Priority Skills; however, you will retain the remaining foundation of your Skill Tree.]
Ther’Abella’s hand froze mid-air.
"Level 555 down to Level 1?!" she choked out, her blood running cold.

Four hundred years... Four hundred years of bleeding in the dust, cracking her bones against monsters, grinding her meridians to powder just to forge her level into a powerful weapon... And this damn system wanted to wipe it clean in a single stroke?
Strip her priority skills? Reduce her to the strength of a newly awakened child?
’Why the hell would I throw four centuries of agony down the drain?!’
Her teeth ground together so hard her jaw ached.
To lose her level was to become weak again... It was to become that helpless squire who stood on the terrace while her Lady was dragged into the dirt...
She stared at the pulsing crimson prompt, and then, slowly, she swallowed the dry lump in her throat.
’Wait.’
A dark calculating thought flickered behind her piercing blue eyes.
’Where is this Lord summoning me?’

If the summoning was taking place in one of the high-tier outer rings, an Unknown Zone or an active sovereign battlefield crawling with high-rank monsters, she wouldn’t need four hundred years to rebuild her stats.

Her martial mastery wasn’t gone, her combat instincts, her blade katas, and her stellar control were carved into her soul so a Level 1 warrior with the reflexes of an apex killer could slaughter high-tier beasts and skyrocket her level in weeks.
’And the Lord,’ she thought, her jaw hardening into stone. ’If this Lord is weak... If this Lord tries to hold me back, tries to use me as an ornamental guard or dictate my path.’
She could kill the Lord.
Break the boundary stone, reclaim her rogue status, and use the territory’s carcass as a launching pad to wage war on Yggdrasil.
"Fine," Ther’Abella growled through her teeth. "Take the levels."
She jabbed her index finger straight into the glowing [ Y ].
BOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOOM!
A colossal vortex of golden light swallowed the tavern room whole.
